fields.foundation: The Akkadian Empire is widely regarded as the world's first true empire: a multi-ethnic, multilingual state governed by a centralised administration over a large territory. Sargon of Akkad founded it around 2334 BCE. According to tradition, Sargon began as cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish, a position that gave him access to the court and administration of one of Sumer's leading city-states. He supplanted Ur-Zababa, founded the city of Akkad as his capital (a city whose precise location has never been identified archaeologically) and then defeated Lugal-zage-si of Uruk, who had unified much of Sumer and was the strongest opponent in the region. In what his inscriptions describe as 34 battles, Sargon brought the Sumerian city-states of southern Mesopotamia under Akkadian control, and after the conquest of the south he symbolically washed his weapons in the Lower Sea, the Persian Gulf. He then campaigned into Elam to the east and up the Euphrates into Syria, reaching the Cedar Forest and the Silver Mountains towards the Mediterranean, while later legend carried his armies into Anatolia. Sargon combined conquest with deliberate cultural integration. He appointed his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur, binding Sumerian religious authority to his dynasty. Enheduanna, who composed elaborate hymns to the goddess Inanna, is often described as the first named author in recorded history. Sargon placed Akkadian officials in the conquered cities and imposed a single administration on what had been a patchwork of competing city-states.
fields.socioeconomy: The Akkadian Empire governed one of the most economically productive regions of the ancient world, the alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia fed by the Tigris and Euphrates, and connected it through trade networks reaching from the Indus Valley Civilisation to the Mediterranean. Sumer's agricultural surplus came from a canal and irrigation system developed over millennia, and it fed both the urban populations of the city-states and the armies of the empire. The Akkadian kings worked to standardise weights and measures and administrative practice across their realm, easing exchange between previously autonomous cities with differing systems. The empire stood at the head of the Persian Gulf and so controlled the maritime route connecting Mesopotamia to Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (the Indus Valley), which brought copper, stone, timber and luxury goods to resource-poor Mesopotamia; Sargon declared that ships from these lands moored at the quay of Akkad. Akkadian became the principal language of royal inscriptions and administration, increasingly displacing Sumerian in everyday written use. The existing Sumerian urban elite kept its place, with an Akkadian imperial class set over it: temple estates, merchants and farming communities carried on much as before, but now paid taxes and tribute to Akkadian governors rather than to independent city-kings. The revolts of Sargon's later reign and of the reigns of Rimush and Naram-Sin suggest that this accommodation was fragile and that imperial demands often exceeded what subject cities considered legitimate.
fields.military: The Akkadian army marked an advance over the city-state armies of the preceding Early Dynastic period. Sumerian warfare had relied heavily on close-order infantry, as depicted on the Standard of Ur and the Stele of the Vultures; Sargon's army appears to have made greater use of lightly equipped troops and archers, which allowed more flexible tactics. The empire kept a permanent force rather than relying solely on seasonal levies, a prerequisite for sustained campaigning over great distances. Sargon's inscriptions record that 5,400 men ate daily in his presence. This is generally understood as a standing royal army, the core around which larger forces were assembled for major campaigns. Akkadian power reached its height under Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin (r. c. 2254–2218 BCE). His Victory Stele, now in the Louvre, depicts him ascending a mountain over the bodies of defeated Lullubi enemies, an image of personal military supremacy that influenced royal iconography for centuries. Naram-Sin's campaigns carried the empire to its greatest extent: he claimed the conquest of Armanum and Ebla in Syria and a victory over the ruler of Magan across the Gulf, and suppressed a great revolt of Sumerian and northern cities. The army's weakness was its dependence on the energy of individual rulers. Rimush and Manishtushu, Sargon's sons, are both said to have been murdered by courtiers, and in the final decades the army could not defend the empire's long frontiers against Gutian incursions, Amorite pressure and internal revolt at the same time.
fields.governance: The Akkadian Empire developed the first known bureaucratic system designed to govern a multi-ethnic territorial state. Many of its practices, including standardised measures, appointed provincial governors and a single written language for imperial administration, were taken up by later Mesopotamian empires. Sargon installed loyal Akkadian officials as governors (ensi) in the conquered Sumerian city-states, placing them alongside or above the existing local and temple authorities to secure revenue and military loyalty. The empire kept detailed written records, including economic tablets, administrative correspondence and royal inscriptions, on a scale and with a uniformity of format not seen before. Naram-Sin carried these developments furthest and added an ideology of divine kingship. He took the title "King of the Four Quarters" and had his name written with the divine determinative, claiming to be the god of Akkad. The claim had no clear precedent in Mesopotamia and turned the king from servant of the gods into a god himself. The cuneiform script, inherited from Sumer, was adapted to write the Semitic Akkadian language and eventually became the administrative script of much of the ancient Near East. The empire never resolved the tension between its centralising ambitions and the autonomy of the Sumerian city-states, whose temples and ruling families had governed themselves for centuries and repeatedly revolted against Akkadian taxation and interference. Rebellions recurred in nearly every reign from Sargon's old age onward.
fields.impact: The Akkadian Empire mattered to later civilisation because it established the pattern of empire, centralised territorial rule over diverse populations, that later Mesopotamian states followed. The Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112–2004 BCE), the Old Babylonian kingdom, the Assyrian Empire and in the end the Achaemenid Empire all drew on administrative, ideological and cultural precedents set in the Akkadian period, and later Mesopotamian kings revered Sargon and Naram-Sin as models of kingship. The Akkadian language, promoted as the language of royal administration, later became in its Babylonian form the diplomatic lingua franca of the ancient Near East for much of the second millennium BCE. It was used in correspondence between Egypt and the Hittites and throughout the Amarna letters of the 14th century BCE. The concept of divine kingship introduced by Naram-Sin, though controversial and later remembered with suspicion, was revived by the kings of Ur III. Enheduanna's compositions, among the earliest attributed literary texts in history, set conventions of religious poetry that influenced Mesopotamian literary culture for centuries. The empire joined Semitic Akkadian and Sumerian traditions, and the combination defined the later course of Mesopotamian civilisation: the Sumerian literary and religious tradition was preserved, elaborated and transmitted through Akkadian. The period also saw major developments in representational art. The best-known example is the naturalistic sculpted portraiture of the copper-alloy head from Nineveh known as the Mask of Sargon, which may represent Sargon or Naram-Sin.
fields.decline: The Akkadian Empire collapsed over roughly 85 years, from Naram-Sin's peak (c. 2240 BCE) to the end of the dynasty (c. 2154 BCE), under military, political and environmental pressures that its institutions could not withstand. The military threat came from the Gutians, a highland people from the Zagros mountains. Their incursions into the Mesopotamian lowlands intensified under Shar-Kali-Sharri and disrupted agriculture and trade while Akkadian armies were tied down in reactive punitive campaigns. Amorite pressure from the western steppe, against which Shar-Kali-Sharri also fought, added further strain. The political weakness was the endemic dynastic instability of the Akkadian state: Rimush and Manishtushu are reported to have been murdered by courtiers, and after Shar-Kali-Sharri's death (c. 2193 BCE) the Sumerian King List records four kings in rapid succession with the line "Who was king? Who was not king?", signalling complete political chaos. The environmental pressure, increasingly emphasised by modern scholarship, was the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, a prolonged drought that struck much of the Near East around 2200 BCE and caused crop failures, famine and population movement. Archaeologists have linked the abandonment of Tell Leilan in northern Syria to this climatic episode, which suggests that the drought was severe enough to undermine the agricultural basis of centralised rule in the north. The city of Akkad itself declined into obscurity, and its location remains unidentified to this day.
fields.summary: The Akkadian Empire, widely regarded as the world's first empire, established organised multi-ethnic territorial rule. The long succession of empires that followed, from the Assyrians to the Persians and beyond, worked within the political form that Sargon of Akkad first defined.
fields.teaser: Founded by Sargon of Akkad around 2334 BCE, the Akkadian Empire is widely regarded as history's first true empire. Sargon's conquests brought the city-states of Sumer and Akkad under a single ruler.
fields.t0: Founded by Sargon of Akkad, it is widely regarded as the world's first empire, uniting the Sumerian city-states under one ruler.
fields.t1: Its governors, standard measures and written Akkadian set the template that later Mesopotamian empires followed.
fields.t2: Gutian raids, palace murders and a severe drought around 2200 BCE brought it down; its capital has never been found.
fields.dyk: Sargon's daughter Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god at Ur, is often described as the first named author in recorded history.
